title: phase-aligned-batch-stripping-experiments
content:
Purpose:
Quick experiment plan + running notes to validate whether coordinated (phase-aligned) request batching across replicas is a primary driver of periodic microburst/backpressure events we see on NVLink/NIC. Idea: intentionally 'strip' or jitter batch start times and observe effect on tail latency, link utilization spikes, and NCCL collective timing.

Background/context:
- Over the last 6 weeks we've seen recurring ~5-20 ms tail spikes in 8x A100 inference pods under steady 80% load. Correlation with NVLink utilization + NCCL allreduce timing suggests that many replicas are hitting collectives in lockstep causing short-lived link saturation.
- Existing notes catalog many microburst phenomena, but less focused on the hypothesis that synchronized batching (same request alignment across replicas) amplifies packetization and queueing.
- This doc is exploratory: lightweight experiments run on staging cluster c-llm-qa (8x A100-80GB, DGX-like topology) to test whether small phasing offsets reduce spike amplitude without hurting throughput.

Hypothesis:
1) When replicas process requests with aligned batch boundaries, collective communications (all-reduce/all-gather) tend to coalesce and create short (~100-300us) but high-intensity link bursts that propagate as queueing to host staging and NICs.
2) Introducing small phase offsets between replica batch start times ("batch stripping") will spread the communication load and reduce tail latency but may slightly reduce CPU/GPU utilization or batching efficiency.
3) There's an optimal offset window (microsecond->millisecond range) where tail reduction is significant while throughput loss is minimal.

Experiment matrix (short):
- Baseline: default runtime batching (no deliberate offset).
- Static offsets: per-replica offsets of {200us, 500us, 1ms, 5ms, 10ms} applied deterministically (replica i offset = i * offset).
- Random jitter: uniform jitter in [0, X] where X in {1ms, 5ms, 10ms}.
- KV-cache alignment tests: same as above but with warm KV cache vs cold cache to see amplification with cache hits.
- Different batch sizes: bs = {1, 4, 8} token-batch-equivalent (keep request qps constant by varying inter-arrival).
- Network stress: repeat each config with synthetic cross-traffic on NIC to emulate tenant noise.

Hardware/stack:
- Cluster: c-llm-qa staging, 8x A100-80GB, NVLink full mesh within host, Mellanox HDR interconnect between hosts (tests mostly single-host but some cross-host).
- OS/kernel: Ubuntu 22.04, NVIDIA driver 535.x, CUDA 12.2, NCCL 2.18.3 (custom tuned knobs used in runtime).
- Runtime: serving-runtime branch batch-stripping-experiments (ref PR 502). Using same request handler used in prod with additional injection hooks.

Instrumentation & metrics captured:
- Per-request latency histogram (p50/p90/p95/p99/p99.9) at the route level (server-side).
- Per-collective start/end timestamps (instrumented in NCCL shim) to compute coalescence windows and variance.
- NVLink utilization sampled at 100us resolution (using nvml + per-link counters where available).
- NIC (RDMA) queue depths and packet drops (from ethtool / Rdma counters).
- GPU occupancy and SM util (nsys sampling, 1ms resolution), host staging queue length, and PCIe utilization.
- Throughput: tokens/s and effective batches/s.

Quick commands used (notes):
- start harness: python scripts/bench_driver.py --qps 1200 --workload long-context --batching runtime --clients 200 --duration 600
- apply offset (runtime flag): --batch-start-offset-ms-per-replica=0.0002  (200us)
- collect nvlink: ./tools/nvlink_sample.sh --interval-us 100 --out nvlink-baseline.csv
- nsys capture stub (sampling): nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --sample=1ms --output=run-<cfg> ...

Baseline observations (summary):
- Baseline p99.9: 54 ms, p99: 28 ms at steady 80% load; occasional 120-220 ms rare spikes every ~60s.
- NVLink samples show short peaks where link utilization jumps to 200-350 GB/s aggregated for 200-400us windows. These align with NCCL collective intervals recorded.
- Host staging queue jumps from 20->400 entries during those windows.

Results (static offset sweep, single-host):
- 200us per-replica offset: p99.9 reduced from 54ms -> 36ms (~33% reduc), p99 -> 22 ms. Throughput unchanged within ±2%. Collective coalescence metric (fraction of collectives happening within 500us across all replicas) fell from 0.72 -> 0.34.
- 500us offset: p99.9 -> 30ms, p99 -> 20ms; slight GPU occupancy variance but throughput -1.7%.
- 1ms offset: p99.9 -> 28ms, p99 -> 19ms; throughput -2.8%.
- 5ms offset: tail continues to improve minimally but batching efficiency loss grows (throughput -6.5%).
- 10ms offset: throughput -12% (too big), tail slightly better than 1ms but not worth cost.
- Random jitter [0,1ms]: similar benefit to deterministic 500us. [0,5ms] reduces tail but at higher throughput cost.

KV-cache sensitivity:
- With warm KV cache, bursts magnified (collective intervals larger) and offsets provided larger relative tail improvements (p99.9 down by up to 50% for 500us offset). Cold cache cases had smaller improvements (because compute-bound stages dominate).

Cross-host runs (small sample):
- When replicas are spread across hosts, optimal offset window widened slightly due to inter-host latencies. 1-5ms offsets had better marginal returns; microburst amplitude measured on per-host NICs differed by host placement.

Anomalies/notes:
- In some runs using deterministic offsets >=1ms we saw transient increase in p50 variance — likely scheduling jitter on CPU threads that shifted batch formation. Need to instrument OS scheduling and request handler batching queues.
- One run showed persistent NCCL timeouts when random jitter was used with very small batch sizes (bs=1); hypothesis: jitter reduced opportunities for intra-rep request coalescing, exposing tiny NCCL handshake failure under current timeout config. Patch NCCL timeouts in PR-502.
- Observed a slight correlation between host CPU frequency governor and effectiveness of offsets: ondemand/powersave made batch dispatch jitterier and diminished benefits; set to performance for tests.

Conclusions so far:
- Phase-aligned batches are a measurable contributor to short-lived interconnect microbursts. Small phase offsets (200-1000us range) reduce tail latency substantially with negligible throughput impact for our typical batch sizes (4-8 tokens-equivalent).
- Warm KV cache amplifies the phenomenon because communication-heavy phases align more strongly across requests.
- Deterministic offsets or small uniform jitter are both effective; deterministic offsets are simpler to reason about for rollouts.

Quick recommendations (for rollout experiments):
- Prototype a runtime flag to enable per-replica deterministic batch start offsets (default disabled). Ramp to 10% of capacity with 500us offsets and monitor p99.9 and throughput for 48 hours.
- Add a sentinel metric: collective-coalescence-ratio (fraction of collectives within 500us) to runtime dashboards to detect regressions.
- Tune NCCL handshake and small-timeout parameters in staged rollout to avoid random-jitter-triggered timeouts.

Next steps / experiments to run:
- Repeat the sweep on production-like commodity nodes (slightly different NVLink configs) to validate transferability.
- Test offset coordination with autoscaling: verify that newly added replicas get offsets assigned deterministically to avoid transient alignment on scale-up.
- Explore adaptive offsets that react to detected coalescence (short term control loop) rather than static config.

Questions for the team / unresolved:
- Does patching runtime to pick per-replica offsets require any coordination with Dedicated deployments where replica placement is customer-controlled? (cc: Solutions eng)
- Are there any compliance or determinism concerns with adding small randomized timing into request handling (audit asked)?

Raw attachments / artifacts stored elsewhere:
- nvlink and collective timing CSVs: gs://redwood-staging/bench/batch-strip/2025-02-14/*
- Raw nsys captures (compressed): gs://redwood-staging/bench/batch-strip/nsys/

Notes-to-self: keep this doc lean. If results hold in rollout we'll convert to a full playbook with rollout steps and rollback flags.

Slack threads: #serving-runtime (refer INF-1823 thread), callout to @ravi for follow-up on sample code in PR-502.

-- Ava
